**Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** is a United Kingdom Act of Parliament that implemented many of the tax measures announced in the Coalition Government’s **June 2010 “Emergency Budget”** after the 2010 general election.

It is one of two major UK Finance Acts passed in 2010: the first was the **Finance Act 2010**, passed under the outgoing Labour Government, and the second was the **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010**, passed under the Conservative–Liberal Democrat Coalition.

## Basic details

- **Short title:** Finance (No. 2) Act 2010  
- **Citation:** **2010 c. 31**  
- **Jurisdiction:** United Kingdom  
- **Royal Assent:** **27 July 2010**  
- **Government:** Conservative–Liberal Democrat Coalition, Chancellor George Osborne  
- **Budget implemented:** June 2010 Emergency Budget  
- **Main subject:** Taxation, public revenue, duties, and related fiscal changes  

The Act’s long title was broadly in the standard Finance Act form: to grant certain duties, alter other duties, amend the law relating to the National Debt and public revenue, and make further provision in connection with finance.

---

# Political and economic context

The Act came shortly after the 2010 general election, which produced a hung Parliament and the formation of the Conservative–Liberal Democrat Coalition Government. The new Government argued that the UK needed a programme of fiscal consolidation following the financial crisis of 2007–08 and the recession.

The June 2010 Emergency Budget combined:

- tax rises, especially on consumption and capital gains;
- reductions in some business taxes;
- personal tax allowance increases;
- anti-avoidance measures;
- reforms intended to support business investment and employment.

The Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 was the legislative vehicle for many of those measures.

---

# Major provisions

## 1. VAT increase to 20%

One of the most significant and politically controversial measures was the increase in the standard rate of **Value Added Tax**.

The Act provided for the standard VAT rate to rise from:

> **17.5% to 20%**

with effect from:

> **4 January 2011**

This was one of the central revenue-raising measures of the Emergency Budget.

The Act also included associated provisions to prevent avoidance and “forestalling”, where businesses might try to structure transactions before the rate rise to benefit from the lower rate.

The VAT increase did **not** affect zero-rated goods such as most food, children’s clothing, books and newspapers, nor exempt supplies such as many financial and insurance services.

---

## 2. Insurance Premium Tax increases

The Act also increased **Insurance Premium Tax**, broadly in line with the VAT rise.

The standard rate of Insurance Premium Tax rose from:

> **5% to 6%**

The higher rate rose from:

> **17.5% to 20%**

These changes also took effect from **4 January 2011**.

Insurance Premium Tax applies to many general insurance products, such as motor insurance, home insurance and travel insurance. The higher rate applies to certain insurance sold with goods and services, for example some travel insurance and appliance insurance.

---

## 3. Capital Gains Tax changes

The Act made important changes to **Capital Gains Tax**, especially for higher-income individuals.

Before the change, most capital gains for individuals were generally taxed at a flat rate of **18%**.

The Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 introduced a higher CGT rate of:

> **28%**

for individuals whose total taxable income and gains exceeded the higher-rate income tax threshold.

In broad terms:

- basic-rate taxpayers continued to pay CGT at **18%** on gains falling within the unused part of their basic-rate band;
- higher-rate and additional-rate taxpayers paid **28%** on gains above that level;
- trustees and personal representatives were generally brought within the higher rate.

The CGT changes took effect from **23 June 2010**, the day after the Emergency Budget.

---

## 4. Entrepreneurs’ Relief expanded

The Act increased the lifetime limit for **Entrepreneurs’ Relief**, a relief allowing qualifying business disposals to be taxed at a reduced CGT rate.

The lifetime limit was increased to:

> **£5 million**

This meant that qualifying gains up to that lifetime amount could benefit from the Entrepreneurs’ Relief rate, which was then **10%**.

This was intended to soften the effect of the CGT rate rise on genuine business owners and entrepreneurs.

Entrepreneurs’ Relief has since been renamed **Business Asset Disposal Relief**, and the lifetime limit has changed in later legislation, but the 2010 Act was a key point in its expansion.

---

## 5. Income tax personal allowance changes

The Act formed part of the Coalition Government’s policy of increasing the income tax personal allowance, especially for lower and middle earners.

For the tax year **2011–12**, the Act increased the basic personal allowance for individuals under 65 to:

> **£7,475**

This was an increase of £1,000 over the previous level.

At the same time, the basic-rate limit was adjusted so that higher-rate taxpayers did not receive the full benefit of the personal allowance increase.

This reflected a major Liberal Democrat policy adopted by the Coalition: moving toward a substantially higher personal allowance.

---

## 6. Corporation tax reforms

The Act included corporation tax changes connected with the Coalition’s plan to make the UK corporate tax system more competitive.

Measures included reductions in corporation tax rates for future financial years.

The main rate of corporation tax was set to fall from:

> **28% to 27%**

for the financial year beginning **1 April 2011**.

The small profits rate was also reduced, moving from:

> **21% to 20%**

from **1 April 2011**.

These were early steps in a broader programme of corporation tax reductions pursued during the Coalition years.

---

## 7. Capital allowances and business tax

The Act included measures relating to capital allowances, which determine how businesses receive tax relief for investment in plant and machinery.

The Government’s wider policy was to reduce headline corporation tax rates while making some capital allowance rules less generous.

Measures associated with the 2010 reforms included changes to:

- writing-down allowances;
- annual investment allowance policy;
- business investment reliefs;
- related computational rules.

Some of the detailed capital allowance changes were phased or dealt with in later Finance Acts, but Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 was part of the legislative foundation of that business tax reform package.

---

## 8. Furnished holiday lettings

The Act dealt with the tax treatment of **furnished holiday lettings**.

Furnished holiday lettings historically received certain favourable tax treatment if they met qualifying conditions. The rules had been under review because of EU law concerns and questions about whether the relief was too generous.

The 2010 legislation preserved and amended the regime rather than abolishing it outright. Later legislation made further changes to qualifying conditions.

---

## 9. Anti-avoidance and tax administration

As with most Finance Acts, the Act contained a range of technical and anti-avoidance provisions.

These included rules addressing:

- tax avoidance schemes;
- disguised or artificial arrangements;
- VAT forestalling around the rate rise;
- corporate tax avoidance;
- capital gains tax planning;
- stamp taxes and transaction-based avoidance;
- information, penalties and compliance matters.

Finance Acts often contain many detailed schedules aimed at closing specific loopholes identified by HM Treasury and HMRC.

---

## 10. Duties and indirect taxes

The Act also made provisions relating to other taxes and duties, including some changes or confirmations concerning:

- alcohol duties;
- tobacco duties;
- fuel duties;
- vehicle excise duty;
- landfill tax;
- climate change levy or environmental taxes;
- gambling duties;
- stamp duty land tax and stamp taxes.

Not every rate change announced in 2010 was necessarily made by this Act alone; some rates are set or altered through other Finance Acts, statutory instruments, or prior legislation. But the Act formed part of the 2010 fiscal package across both direct and indirect taxes.

---

# Relationship with other Finance Acts

## Finance Act 2010

The **Finance Act 2010** was passed earlier in the year, before the change of Government. It implemented measures from the March 2010 Budget of the Labour Government.

## Finance (No. 2) Act 2010

The **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** implemented the Coalition Government’s June 2010 Emergency Budget.

The “No. 2” title simply indicates that it was the second Finance Act in that calendar year.

## Later Finance Acts

Some policies announced in the Emergency Budget were implemented not in the Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 but in later Acts, especially the **Finance Act 2011**. For example, the permanent **bank levy** was legislated later, though it was part of the same broad fiscal strategy.

---

# Significance

The Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 is significant because it marked the first major tax legislation of the Coalition Government and reflected the policy direction of the early 2010s:

1. **Fiscal consolidation** after the financial crisis.  
2. **Higher VAT** as a major revenue-raising measure.  
3. **Higher CGT for higher earners**, partly to reduce income-to-capital conversion incentives.  
4. **Lower corporation tax rates**, designed to improve UK competitiveness.  
5. **Higher personal allowance**, aimed at reducing tax for low and middle earners.  
6. Continued use of detailed anti-avoidance legislation.

The Act is particularly remembered for the rise in VAT to **20%**, which remains the UK standard VAT rate today.

---

# In short

**Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** was the UK Act that gave legal effect to much of George Osborne’s June 2010 Emergency Budget. Its best-known provisions were:

- increasing VAT from **17.5% to 20%**;
- increasing Insurance Premium Tax;
- raising Capital Gains Tax to **28%** for higher-rate taxpayers;
- increasing the Entrepreneurs’ Relief lifetime limit to **£5 million**;
- raising the income tax personal allowance for 2011–12;
- beginning reductions in corporation tax rates;
- introducing various business tax, anti-avoidance and administrative tax measures.
